title: We said we'd work on it this year and nothing changed
summary: You both agreed to work on it, and a year later nothing changed. Why "we'll work on it" feels like a plan but isn't, and how to make the next try real.
body_markdown:
Sometime around last January, maybe on a long drive or late one night after a bad week, the two of you had a real conversation. It went well, actually. You both admitted things weren't right. Your partner didn't get defensive. Somebody said "okay, we'll work on it," and the other one said "yeah, we will," and you went to bed feeling closer than you had in months.


Now it's almost the end of the year and you can't point to a single thing that's different.


If that's where you are, here's the uncomfortable, slightly hopeful answer: it's very possible nobody lied. "We'll work on it" usually isn't a promise that got broken. It's a promise that was never shaped enough to keep.


## The belief that makes this so painful


The assumption most people carry is simple. If my partner really agreed, and really meant it, then something would have changed. Since nothing changed, either they didn't mean it or they don't care enough.


That logic feels airtight. It's also usually wrong, or at least incomplete.


Agreeing that there's a problem and knowing what to do on a Tuesday night are completely different things. "We need to be closer." "We should stop fighting about money." "I'll be more present." Every one of those is sincere, and none of them tells a tired person what to actually do differently at 7pm when the kids are melting down and the dishwasher is making that noise again. So the intention sits there, fully meant and completely unused, while the old habits run the house.


The feeling of having agreed is a real feeling. It just isn't a plan. And because it feels so much like one, it can stand in for a plan for twelve months without anyone noticing.


## The detail that shows up a few messages in


When someone brings this to Maia, there's a detail that comes up again and again, usually a few messages in: they've had the "we should work on it" conversation more than once. Sometimes three or four times across the year. Each one felt productive. Each one ended with relief.


And that relief is the tell. The conversation itself became the repair. Talking about changing released enough pressure that nobody had to actually change, the same way[an apology can reset the tension without fixing anything](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/my-partner-apologizes-but-nothing-changes) . By late in the year, people aren't mostly angry about the original problem anymore. They're angry that they got their hopes up again, and a little embarrassed that they keep falling for their own good conversations.


If that's you, it's worth being gentle with yourself. You didn't fall for anything. You did the part most couples never do, which is admit there's a problem. You just stopped one step short of the part that makes it real.


## How to tell a vague promise from a partner who won't show up


These two situations feel the same from the inside, so it's worth separating them before you decide what a year of nothing means.


- **Nothing was ever specific.** Neither of you could have said, in one sentence, what "working on it" looked like. There was no behavior to do, so there was no behavior to skip. This is the common one, and it's fixable.
- **Something specific was agreed, and it didn't happen.** "I'll stop checking my phone at dinner." "We'll do a real date every other Friday." It was clear, it was small, and it still didn't happen, repeatedly, without any real attempt. That's a different signal.
- **Only one of you was ever going to do the work.** "We'll work on it" quietly meant "you'll keep bringing it up." If you've been the only one planning, reminding, and reopening,[that imbalance is its own problem](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/im-the-only-one-trying-in-my-relationship) and deserves its own conversation.


Most couples are in the first bucket, even when it feels like the second. Be honest about which one you're actually in before you treat a vague year as proof of bad faith.


## Turning "work on it" into something you can actually do


If you want the next attempt to be different, don't have the same good conversation again. Have a smaller, more boring one.


1. **Pick one thing, not the relationship.** "Us" is not something you can work on. "We check in for ten minutes on Sunday night" is. Choose the one change that would matter most, even if it feels too small.
2. **Make it visible.** A good test: could someone watching your week tell whether it happened? If not, it's still a feeling, not a behavior.
3. **Each of you owns a piece.** Not "you need to be more affectionate." Something like: I'll stop starting money conversations after 9pm, you'll tell me when you need a day before we decide. Two small commitments, one each.
4. **Plan for the week it slips.** It will slip. Decide now what you'll say when it does, so a missed Sunday becomes "hey, we skipped it, tonight?" and not a referendum on the whole relationship.
5. **Set a check-in date that isn't New Year's.** Six weeks is enough time to see whether anything is moving. A year is enough time to lose track of what you agreed to.


This is less romantic than the late-night talk. That's the point. Couples who actually change tend to have unglamorous agreements, and they tend to[stop reopening the same argument](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) precisely because there's finally something concrete to point to.


## If you do all of that and it still doesn't move


Then you've learned something you couldn't learn from a year of vague promises. If the change was clear, small, fairly shared, and your partner still doesn't try, the question is no longer about planning. It's about willingness, and no amount of better structure fixes that. Some people reach that point and decide to keep going on different terms. Some start asking whether[this should be the year they finally leave](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/should-this-be-the-year-i-leave) . Both are honest places to land, and you'll be deciding with real information instead of a year of hoping.


But don't skip to that verdict yet if the last twelve months never had anything concrete in them. Most "nothing changed" years weren't a test your partner failed. They were a test nobody wrote.


If you want help figuring out what the one specific thing should be, and how to say it so your partner hears a plan rather than another complaint, that's a good conversation to have with Maia first. Bring the real details: what you agreed to, what actually happened, and what you'd need to see by spring to feel like this year was different.
